paragraphs: (1) In the Mishnah: Berakhot 2:2; Peah 3:6; Rosh Hashanah 4:4 (31b); Nedarim 3:11; Sanhedrin 7:5.

(2) In the final chapter of Bekhorot, 58a, Ben Azzai said: ‘All Israel’s sages are like a garlic peel, except for this bald one,’ meaning Rabbi Akiva. Rashi explains that Rabbi Yehoshua was his son, and therefore was called ben Korchah. Rashbam and the Arukh write likewise. We find that Rabbi Akiva had a son named Rabbi Yehoshua: Shevuot 6a. In the Jerusalem Talmud there, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva’s son, asked Rabbi Akiva. [Rashi explains, on the parallel Bavli passage, that this was Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah.] In the Tosefta, Negaim, chapter 1, Rabbi Yose said: ‘Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva’s son, asked.’ Also in Pesachim; see above. In the Tosefta, Ketubbot, at the locator פ״ר, and in the Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Af Al Pi, halakhah 2: an incident concerning Rabbi Yehoshua son of Rabbi Akiva, who married a woman and stipulated with her that he would neither feed nor support her; rather, she would feed and support him and teach him Torah. Tosafot in Bekhorot there object: was it so hateful to mention Rabbi Akiva by name that one should mention him by a derogatory expression, as in ‘Go up, bald one’? See what is written in Asarah Maamarot, the discourse Chikkur Din, part 5, section 14 [chapter 11 in the checked text], under Rabbi Akiva, and you will see that it is not a derogatory name. In Shabbat 152a that heretic said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah, ‘How far is it from here to Baldtown?’ and intended an insult. In Megillah 28a Rabbi asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah: ‘Through what did you merit long life?’ Rabbi also asked him, ‘Bless me.’ He replied: ‘May it be the divine will that you attain half my years.’ How can one say that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was Rabbi Akiva’s son? Rabbi Akiva was forty when he married Kalba Savua’s daughter and lived 120 years; when Rabbi Akiva died, Rabbi was born. Even if Rabbi Yehoshua had been born in the first year of Rabbi Akiva’s marriage to Kalba Savua’s daughter, he would have been only eighty when Rabbi was born. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was at least 140 when he blessed Rabbi to attain half his years, meaning seventy: he would not have blessed him with less than seventy, for ‘the days of our years are seventy years.’ Rabbi was then sixty. That is, Rabbi was born when Rabbi Akiva died, when Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was eighty; from eighty to 140 is sixty years. Thus, when Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah blessed him to attain half his years, namely seventy, he blessed him with only ten years. What sort of blessing is that? Moreover, it seems reasonable that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was not born immediately when Rabbi Akiva married Kalba Savua’s daughter, when Rabbi Akiva was forty, but only after Rabbi Akiva had spent twelve years and another twelve years, totaling twenty-four, studying Torah before the marriage. When he returned home after twenty-four years and married her, Rabbi Akiva was sixty-four. If Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was born when Rabbi Akiva was sixty-four, he was fifty-six at Rabbi Akiva’s death, since from sixty-four to 120 is fifty-six. Thus, when Rabbi was born on the day Rabbi Akiva died, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was fifty-six. It has already been demonstrated that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah could not have been less than 140 when he blessed Rabbi to attain half his years. Rabbi must therefore have been eighty-four, since from fifty-six to 140 is eighty-four. Thus, when Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was 140, Rabbi was already older than half his years: half of 140 is only seventy, while Rabbi was then eighty-four. Rabbenu Nissim, in Megillat Setarim, who found in Bereshit Rabbah that Ben Azzai’s ‘except for the bald one’ referred to Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, as cited in Tosafot, the chapter Yesh Nochalin, explains that Korchah was Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, who, the Jerusalem Talmud says, was bald. [I did not find it.] Rabbenu Tam explains that it is a person’s name. End quotation. So too Tosafot, Shabbat 150a: it was not Rabbi Akiva, but another man whose name was Korchah. Korach is a personal name, like Korach. [But this is difficult, for one does not name someone after a wicked person.] Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was born long before Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva’s son. End quotation. So too Tosafot, Yesh Nochalin, 113a. The conclusion emerging from Tosafot is that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was not Rabbi Akiva’s son. This also seems reasonable: had he been Rabbi Akiva’s son, it should have said ‘son of the bald one,’ as a descriptive epithet. Moreover, would his son forever be called this merely because Ben Azzai happened to call Rabbi Akiva bald once? In the baraita in the chapter Chelek, Rabbi Yehudah ben Korchah is mentioned: perhaps he was his brother, or was bald. Although there is also a Rabbi Ammi bar Korchah—see his entry—there is no room to suppose that he was Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah’s brother, since Rabbi Ammi bar Korchah spoke in Rav’s name. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah lived long, was Rabbi’s teacher, and lived twice Rabbi’s years; see his entry. But this is difficult: who told him this prophecy? Although he blessed Rabbi to attain half his years, who can say that Rabbi did not live beyond half his years? Furthermore, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah blessed Rabbi to attain half the years he had reached then. Perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah lived many years after that blessing. Even if the blessing was fulfilled, and Rabbi lived half the years he had then reached, Rabbi’s lifespan would still not equal half the full years Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah lived after the blessing. The difficulty grows in light of what Tosafot write in Af Al Pi, 62b, concerning the statement: Rabbi Akiva was Kalba Savua’s shepherd. His daughter saw that he was modest and worthy. She told him, ‘If I become betrothed to you, will you go to the study house?’ He said yes. She became secretly betrothed to him and sent him away, and so forth. He spent twelve years in the study house and brought back twelve thousand students, and so forth. She said, ‘If he listened to me, he would stay another twelve years.’ He said, ‘I am acting with permission,’ and returned for another twelve years, and so forth. Rabbi Akiva’s daughter also did this for Ben Azzai, and so forth: ‘A ewe follows a ewe,’ and so forth. Tosafot write: ‘She saw that he was modest and worthy.’ But in Ellu Overin, 49b, Rabbi Akiva said: ‘When I was an unlearned person, I would say: Give me a Torah scholar, and I shall bite him like a donkey.’ This implies that he was not worthy. One may answer that it was not because he hated a Torah scholar, but because he thought that they acted arrogantly toward the unlearned on account of their Torah, and that the Torah scholars hated them. They also would not let him touch them, because the clothing of the unlearned conveys midras impurity to those who observe purity. Nevertheless, he observed the commandments. Rabbenu Tam. End quotation. But according to Rabbenu Tam’s explanation that he observed the commandments while unlearned, how did he remain unmarried until forty? In Niddah and Kiddushin 29b it says that once a man has reached twenty without marrying, the Holy One, blessed be He, says, ‘May his bones burst,’ and all his days are spent in sinful thoughts. There in Kiddushin, Rav Chisda told Rav Hamnuna: ‘Do not appear before me until you have married.’ Chiddushei Aggadot writes that it is forbidden to look at a wicked person’s face; since he had not married, he considers him wicked because all his days are spent in sinful thoughts. That is why he said, ‘Do not appear before me.’ End quotation. My eyes lit up when I saw in the Mishnah, Yadayim, chapter 3, ‘Rabbi Yochanan ben Yeshua, son of Rabbi Akiva’s father-in-law’; so too Rabbah, at the beginning of Chazit. Accordingly, he had a wife who was Yeshua’s daughter. One may therefore say that he married Yeshua’s daughter at eighteen, the age for marriage. Reliable evidence that he had a wife while still unlearned is found in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, beginning of chapter 6: ‘What were Rabbi Akiva’s beginnings? They said: he was forty and had learned nothing. Once he stood at the mouth of a well and asked, “Who hollowed out this stone?” They told him, “The water which constantly falls upon it,”’ and so forth. Rabbi Akiva immediately reasoned a fortiori: if something soft hollowed out something hard, how much more will words of Torah, which are hard as iron, engrave themselves upon my heart, which is flesh and blood! He immediately returned to learn Torah, he and his son. They sat to learn Torah with teachers of children. He said: ‘Master, teach me Torah.’ Rabbi Akiva held one end of the tablet and his son the other end. He wrote aleph-bet for him, and he learned it; aleph-tav, and he learned it; Torat Kohanim, and he learned it, and so forth. Rabbi Akiva will one day establish the guilt of all the poor in judgment. If they are asked why they did not study and say, ‘Because we were poor,’ we tell them: ‘Was not Rabbi Akiva poor and destitute?’ If they say, ‘Because of our little children,’ we tell them: ‘Did not Rabbi Akiva have many sons and daughters, whom he supported together with his wife Rachel?’ See there. Perhaps his first wife died when he married Kalba Savua’s daughter, and he supported his children from his first wife together with his wife Rachel. One may say that Rachel was Kalba Savua’s daughter; hence their sweetly phrased hint that his daughter likewise did this for Ben Azzai—‘A ewe follows a ewe’—for her name was Rachel. See Rabbi Akiva. According to the wording in the chapter HaNoder, 50a, Rabbi Akiva became betrothed to Kalba Savua’s daughter; her father heard and forbade her by vow from benefiting from any of his property. She went and married him in winter, and so forth. She told him, ‘Go to the study house,’ and so forth. Before he went, he was supporting his children from his first wife and his second wife Rachel. That is why the children are mentioned first in ‘Rabbi Akiva had many sons and daughters, whom he supported, and his wife Rachel’; it should otherwise have said ‘He supported his wife and children.’ Understand this. It is thus demonstrated that he had sons and daughters when he was poor. According to Tosafot’s view that he married Kalba Savua’s daughter twenty-four years after betrothing her, he was then wealthy, for as soon as Rabbi Akiva arrived with twenty-four thousand students, Kalba Savua gave him half his fortune, as related in Af Al Pi. Even if you say that he married her immediately upon betrothal, she became pregnant immediately, and he immediately left to study Torah and did not return home for twenty-four years, whence did he have many sons and daughters? Necessarily these children were born before he married Kalba Savua’s daughter. One may therefore say that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was Rabbi Akiva’s son from his first wife, the daughter of his father-in-law Yeshua, whom Rabbi Akiva married at eighteen. Rabbi Akiva was then poor; hence his son Rabbi Yehoshua stipulated with his wife that he would not feed her. There is some supporting hint in his naming his son Yehoshua after his father-in-law Yeshua. Accordingly, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was born when Rabbi Akiva was eighteen, nineteen, or twenty. Thus, when Rabbi Akiva died, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was a hundred. When he blessed Rabbi, Rabbi was sixty, and so forth; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was then 160, since Rabbi was born when Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was a hundred. Half of 160 is eighty; hence he blessed him to attain half his years. With this, all Tosafot’s objections to Rashi are removed, and the words of Rashi, Rashbam, and the Arukh, who wrote that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was Rabbi Akiva’s son, stand firm and established.

I have further slight supporting evidence that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was Rabbi Akiva’s son. In Shabbat 152a, that eunuch—he was a Sadducee eunuch—said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah: ‘How far is it from here to Baldtown?’ That is, how many stages of travel are there from here to the bald one; he intended to provoke him about his baldness. He replied: ‘As far as from here to Eunuchtown’—as from here to the eunuch. The Sadducee said: ‘A bald goat costs four’—a goat, which is not clothed in wool like a ewe, is called bald. He replied: ‘A castrated sheep costs eight’—a sheep whose testicles have been removed. The Sadducee saw that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was not wearing shoes and told him: ‘One who rides a horse is a king; one who rides a donkey is a free man; one with shoes on his feet is a human being. One with neither this nor that—a man dug into the ground and buried is better than he.’ See there. Kohelet Rabbah, on the verse ‘I have seen servants riding,’ and so forth, relates that a certain heretic said these things to Rabbi Akiva. Thus Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah walked without shoes. In Pesachim 112a: ‘The rabbis taught: Rabbi Akiva commanded his son Rabbi Yehoshua seven things.’ Heilprin cites Rashbam and Tosafot for identifying him as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah [Tosafot reports Rashbam’s interpretation and then objects to the use of the epithet], and so forth, as it says at its end [בסופה; referent uncertain]: ‘All Israel’s sages are like a garlic peel, except for this bald one.’ Yuchasin likewise writes ‘as related in Sotah.’ But search and investigate: you will not find this in Sotah, only in Bekhorot there. Afterwards I saw that the new Talmud edition had corrected it to ‘as related in Bekhorot.’ ‘My son, do not sit in the high part of the town’—so that passersby should not interrupt, Rashi [Rashbam in the checked text]. Incidentally, one may ask whether the reason was instead like Rabbi’s decree that students should not be taught in the marketplace, because of ‘the curves of your thighs’: just as the thigh is concealed, so words of Torah should be concealed, as in Moed Katan 16a. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was Rabbi’s teacher; Rabbi saw that Rabbi Akiva instructed his son Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah not to study in the high part of town, and therefore he too decreed that they should not teach in the marketplace. ‘Do not live in a town whose leaders are Torah scholars, and do not keep shoes off your feet,’ and so forth. This is puzzling: why did Rabbi Akiva need to warn and command him not to leave his feet without shoes? In Shabbat 129a, Rav Yehudah said in Rav’s name: ‘A person should always sell his house’s beams and buy shoes for his feet.’ Rather, this is precisely the point: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was his son, whom that Sadducee eunuch saw walking without shoes. We may infer that he went barefoot. Perhaps this had been his habit from youth, when Rabbi Akiva was poor; hence he needed to command him not to keep shoes off his feet. But this requires examination. According to Rashi’s explanation cited above, he was called Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah because Rabbi Akiva was called bald; yet in the eunuch incident, the description of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah as a bald goat implies that he himself was bald. He should have been called Yehoshua Korchah. One may answer that this would have been derogatory, but because his father Rabbi Akiva was also called ‘this bald one,’ he was called Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah. Alternatively, perhaps Ben Azzai really called Rabbi Akiva bald because he lacked hair, like his son Rabbi Yehoshua. There is supporting evidence from the Kohelet midrash cited above. There is further slight support that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was Rabbi Akiva’s son. In Chelek, 110b: ‘The wilderness generation has no portion in the world to come’: Rabbi Akiva’s words. Rabbi Eliezer says that they do have a portion, for it says, ‘Gather to Me My faithful ones, those who make My covenant.’ Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah says: ‘This verse was spoken only of the righteous in every generation: “those who make My covenant over sacrifice.” “Those who make My covenant” are Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah; “over sacrifice” are Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues, who surrendered themselves to slaughter for words of Torah.’ Thus Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah disagrees with Rabbi Eliezer and follows his father Rabbi Akiva. ‘A son honors his father’; therefore he expounded ‘over sacrifice’ concerning his father Rabbi Akiva. But this requires examination, for he should have said: ‘“Over sacrifice” is my father and his colleagues.’

(3) In the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah: Tosefta, Kelim, Bava Batra 2, and Negaim, chapter 7. Rabbi Elazar ben Taddai lived in his time. He sent Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon the message ‘Vinegar, son of wine’: Bava Metzia 83b. Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin transmitted in his name. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah’s name: Bava Kamma 38b, Megillah 14, Nazir 23b, and Horayot 11. [The latter three passages give Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin.] And Chanan ben Pinchas; Rabbi Chanina son of Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh lived in his time. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah was Rabbi’s colleague: so writes Yuchasin at its end, in the sequence of transmission, from Sefer Yesod Olam. But I brought above Rabbi’s words to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah: ‘Our master, bless me.’ He went to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri: Jerusalem Talmud, Kilayim 4:4 [4:2:3 in the checked text] and Sukkah 1:1. Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Yehudah spoke to him: Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah 1:1. And Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Berokah; Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman taught in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah’s name: Kohelet Rabbah, on ‘Vanity of vanities.’ And Rabbi Shimon: Avodah Zarah 7b, beginning, and Bekhorot 31a. He was sitting with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi’s father: Bava Metzia 84b. Rabbi Tanchuma transmitted in his name. A certain gentile questioned him: Bereshit Rabbah, chapters 13 and 27; Shemot Rabbah, chapter 2; Vayikra Rabbah, chapter 4.
